implementation_notes: Ruby ships the pattern as a mix-in: `include Observable` provides add_observer(observer, func = :update), delete_observer(s), the changed gate that must be set before notification, and notify_observers(*args), which calls each observer's method in insertion order and then clears the changed flag. An observer is any object responding to the method, or a lambda registered with :call, so the Observer interface disappears while the subject stays a normal domain object. Since Ruby 3.0 the library is a bundled gem (ruby/observer) rather than part of the core standard library, so it must be in the Gemfile. Use ActiveSupport::Notifications or a plain array of lambdas when you want named events rather than per-object observers.
code_sketch:
class PriceTicker
  include Observable
  def price=(next_price)
    return if next_price == @price
    @price = next_price
    changed                    # gate: notify_observers does nothing without it
    notify_observers(next_price)
  end
end
warn_low = ->(price) { puts "below limit: #{price}" }
ticker.add_observer(warn_low, :call)
pitfalls: notify_observers is a no-op until changed has been called, and it resets the flag afterwards: a second notification without a fresh changed() silently disappears.

The observer registry is a plain Hash keyed by the observer object - a strong reference. Observers that must not be duplicated or kept alive have to be removed explicitly (delete_observer) or wrapped.
The module does not synchronise: mutating the observer hash from another thread while notifying raises 'can't add a new key into hash during iteration' or loses registrations.
Observers run synchronously in insertion order on the notifying thread; an exception in one observer aborts the remaining observers.
